💬 New Blog Post on Enacted U.S. AI Laws! FPF released a new blog post and chart, Enacted State AI Laws 2023-2025, identifying the 27 enacted AI laws across 14 states from 2023-25, highlighting key compliance requirements and consumer rights, major legislative trends, and effective dates. Notably, most enacted AI laws are already effective as of 2026, requiring entities to begin navigating compliance obligations.

 

Stuff from the States 

 

Alabama - ASAA Signed by Governor (HB 161): Governor Ivey signed this bill into law on February 17. The Act has an effective date of January 1, 2027. The substance of this law largely aligns with the age verification and VPC obligations included in the Texas, Utah, and Louisiana ASAA laws passed last year, but with a few key differences including: extending age verification and parental consent requirements to existing accounts, requiring parental consent for pre-installed apps, removing application exemptions, and adopting a definition for “in-app purchases” clarifying that the term only applies to purchases billed through an app store (e.g., purchases of virtual currencies or digital goods). Notably, the law does not include a private right of action.

 

California - The bill introduction deadline is today, February 20, so we will cover any last-second bill filings in next week’s update. In the meantime, there was no shortage of action in California. 

  • CCPA Consumer Rights Method Bill Introduced (SB 1104): Sen. Cabaldon (D) introduced a bill that would require a business that does not operate exclusively online to offer an email address for submitting consumer rights requests in addition to a telephone number. 
  • Delete Act Amendment on Timing Introduced (SB 1106): Sen. Cabaldon (D) also introduced a Delete Act amendment that would require data brokers to comply with deletion requests within 30 days rather than 45. 
  • CCPA Whistleblowers Bill Introduced (AB 2021): Asm. Schiavo (D) introduced a bill that would allow individuals to submit whistleblower complaints to CalPrivacy alleging violations of the CCPA, with the individual receiving 15-33% of the fine collected if certain criteria are met. This topic was among CalPrivacy's legislative priorities for 2026. 
  • “Digital Choice Act” Introduced (AB 2169): Similar to a bill introduced in Virginia this session (VA SB 85), Asm. Lowenthal introduced a “Digital Choice Act” that would amend the CCPA to add obligations with respect to AI and social media, including: requiring a social media company or a person that deploys an artificial intelligence model to allow a consumer to request a copy of the consumer’s personal information, contextual data, and social graph; requiring a model operator to implement a third-party-accessible interoperability interface to allow a user to share the user’s contextual data directly with other AI models as the user designates.
  • Upcoming CalPrivacy Board Meeting: The agenda and meeting materials are up for CalPrivacy’s first board meeting of the year, happening next week on February 27. Topics include welcoming a new board member, a discussion on a petition to amend existing regulations to incorporate frameworks for “minimal functional mode” and a “tiered consent structure” for general purpose consumer devices, and updates on the DROP system, legislation, and regulation. 

 

Kansas - ASAA Bill Passes Senate (SB 372): This bill was passed by the Senate on February 18 with amendments. Notable Senate amendments to the bill include amending the definition of “account holder” to clarify an individual must be associated with the device and create or maintain an app store account, adding in a definition for in-app purchases (limiting the meaning of that term to purchase of digital currency or goods, etc.), clarifying the effective date as January 1, 2027, and removing the proposed private right of action. The bill now moves to the House for consideration.

 

Kentucky

  • “Kids Code” Amendment Introduced (HB 633): Introduced by Rep. Grossl (R) on February 12, this bill would amend Kentucky’s comprehensive privacy law to incorporate South Carolina and Nebraska design code-style protections for minors, including requiring high-level privacy and safety settings by default, providing accessible tools allowing minors to opt-out of algorithmic recommendation systems except when a minor explicitly requests certain content, and providing parents with controls and oversight of a minor’s settings and account use. In addition to protections, this bill would also establish certain processing restrictions, including restricting use of minors’ personal data for profiling, prohibiting targeted advertising, and prohibiting use of “dark patterns directed at a minor.”
  • ASAA Bill Introduced (HB 632): Introduced by Rep. Dietz (R) on February 12, this bill would establish an App Store Accountability Act framework aligning with the models enacted in Utah, Louisiana, and Texas in 2025.

 

New Hampshire - House Passes Comprehensive Privacy Amendment (HB 1460): The New Hampshire House voted 214-145 to pass an amendment to the state’s comprehensive privacy law. This bill would prohibit a controller from selling “the location and other sensitive data regarding children.” Currently, the law defines “personal data collected from a known child” as sensitive data. The bill has yet to pass the Senate. 

 

New Jersey - Youth Privacy Priority for New Governor: The Kids Mental Health and Online Safety Transition Action Team for New Jersey Governor Sherrill released a report with policy recommendations for protecting kids online. Among the legislative recommendations are: implementing an Age-Appropriate Design Code (modeled on Maryland, Nebraska, and Vermont) with a private right of action, prohibiting under 16s from using social media services with “addictive” features, subjecting AI chatbots to strict liability for promoting harmful content to young people (e.g., suicidal ideation, substance use), and passing a Delete Act-style data broker law.  

 

Oklahoma - House Passes Comprehensive Privacy Bill (SB 546): The House voted to amend and pass a Virginia-style comprehensive privacy bill. The amendment is narrow—it adds a new exemption for compliance with the federal Controlled Substances Act and pushes the effective date to January 1, 2027. The bill has to return to the Senate for a concurrence vote.

 

Oregon - Data Broker Bill Narrowed in Committee (SB 1587): Sen. Campos’s (D) data broker bill was narrowed in committee to prohibit a public body from disclosing personally identifiable information to a data broker unless the data broker first provides a written attestation that the information will not be sold or otherwise transferred to any entity that will use the information to enforce federal immigration law. Originally, the bill would have more broadly prohibited data brokers from providing brokered personal data to any person or entity if the data broker has reason to believe that the person will use the data (directly or indirectly) for purpose related to enforcement of civil law.

 

South Dakota - ASAA Bill Amended & Passed Out of Committee (HB 1275): The State Affairs committee passed this bill with amendments on February 18, including requiring app stores to prevent minors from downloading or purchasing a developer’s app if requested by a developer and clarifying that developers are not prohibited from allowing a parent to customize age-related restrictions, safety features, and settings.

 

Utah - ASAA Law Amendment Passed Out of Committee With Substitute (HB 498): The House Economic Development and Workforce Services Committee passed this bill with amendments on February 18, removing exceptions for developers of “family account applications,” narrowing the “significant changes” definition, adding new requirements for pre-installed apps and existing accounts, and clarifying that developers are not prohibited from allowing a parent to customize age-related restrictions, safety features, and settings from mandatory defaults in minor accounts. If this bill is successfully enacted, these changes could impact the CCIA’s recently filed lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the Act.

 

West Virginia - BIPA-style Bill Introduced (HB 5567): Del. Kimble (R) introduced a bill on February 16 that would enact a Biometric Information Privacy Act regulating the collection, capture, purchase, retention, and use of biometric identifiers and biometric information by private entities.
